Policy stance remains clearly restrictive (funds rate held at 5.25–5.50% and QT ongoing) while acknowledging solid activity and modest disinflation. However, the latest SLOOS points to tighter credit supply and softer loan demand, which tempers the positive read-through:
- Banks report tightening across C&I and consumer products (credit cards, autos), including wider loan spreads and higher minimum credit-score requirements, alongside weaker C&I loan demand.
- CRE lending standards tightened at large, other, and foreign banks, with additional constraints such as lower LTVs, higher DSCRs, and smaller loan sizes.
- Banks cite the economic outlook, reduced risk tolerance, liquidity positions, industry-specific issues, and supervisory/legislative factors as reasons for tightening.

These SLOOS findings imply restrictive financial conditions are still biting and could weigh on growth despite resilient real activity, reinforcing a cautious stance rather than a dovish one. Adjusting for the tighter credit supply signaled by SLOOS, I nudge the sentiment down from mildly positive toward neutral.
